# To Know is Not to Believe

```{=tex}
\epigraph{
\begin{quotepara}
In the beginning, there was a void in the minds of creatures, who moved blindly through the world. And the force of evolution said: ``Let there be sensation,'' and sensation came to be.

From the primordial soup arose beings who could detect light from darkness, warmth from cold. And evolution saw that it was adaptive, and it was good.

And evolution spoke again, saying: ``Let there be more subtle discernment among the creatures.'' And eyes formed to see detail, ears to hear distant sounds, noses to smell food and danger, tongues to taste what nourishes and what harms, and skin to feel the textures of the world.

And Nature called sensation knowledge, and ignorance it called death. And perception and survival were the first day of knowing.

These senses multiplied and refined across generations. Those who sensed well lived to breed, and those who sensed poorly perished. Thus was empirical knowledge selected and preserved.

And in the fullness of time arose creatures who walked upright, whose brains grew large with sensory processing. They began to pass their empirical knowledge to their young through teaching and tale. They named the stars and tracked the seasons. They learned which plants heal and which harm. They studied the ways of prey and predator.

And from these foundations of sensory truth, they built great towers of understanding. They created science and philosophy, art and mathematics. But all rested upon the bedrock of empirical knowing that evolution had wrought.

Thus was empiricism established as the first way of knowing, from which all other knowing springs. And evolution saw all that it had made, and behold, it was very good.
\end{quotepara}
}
```

## Introduction to Knowing {#sec-knowing}

Developing an understanding about how we acquire, validate, and systematise knowledge is an important challenge in philosophy. Philosophers from antiquity to the modern era have grappled with what it means to 'know': from Plato’s forms, Aristotle’s categories, Descartes’ *cogito*, Locke’s *tabula rasa*, Kant’s synthetic *a priori*, and towards contemporary thinking in evolutionary epistemology. In this chapter, I explore some of the most relevant epistemic frameworks that shape our comprehension of reality. What I want to achieve is an appreciation of how these various ways of knowing inform and influence modern scientific practice.

Science is a wholly human endeavour, and as such, it is subject to the same epistemic constraints and biases that affect all human knowledge. How did we come to develop the kind of knowing that only humans have? In this chapter, I want to arrive at this end point by setting the following core inquiry: what is the nature of 'knowledge' for beings at varying levels of complexity, from non-conscious chemical-sensing entities to fully conscious, sentient humans? But I want to accomplish more than that. I also want to explore the evolutionary process by which knowledge has been selected and preserved in the natural world. Naturally, I need to juxtapose these ways of knowing with routes to not knowing, or believing, as the case may be.

The concept of **knowing** requires distinctions between mere *belief*, *justified opinion*, and *genuine knowledge*. At its core, knowing is traditionally characterised as **justified true belief** (JTB). JBT is foundational in epistemology, but it is incomplete. **Edmund Gettier** (1927--2021) challenged this framework in *Is Justified True Belief Knowledge* (1963) by demonstrating that a belief can be justified, true, and believed yet still fail to qualify as knowledge if its truth is coincidental or accidental. His counterexamples, such as the case of the stopped clock[^1_1] and the Smith and Jones[^1_2] case, reveal that justification, truth, and belief, while necessary, are not sufficient conditions for knowledge. Cutting-edge definitions of knowledge now aim to refine JTB by incorporating elements that prevent accidental truths from counting as knowledge. They emphasise that knowledge must be gained in a way that is not just only justified and true, but also epistemically secure, well-grounded, and robust against the kind of coincidences Gettier cases highlight.

[^1_1]: A person looks at a clock to determine the time and sees that it is 3:00. The clock has stopped, but coincidentally, it is actually 3:00 at that moment. The person’s belief that “It is 3:00” is true, justified (based on the clock’s reading), and believed, but it is true only by chance. Hence, it fails to constitute knowledge.

[^1_2]: Smith has strong evidence to believe the proposition: “Jones will get the job, and Jones has ten coins in his pocket”. This evidence might include testimony or observations. From this, Smith deduces: “The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket”. Unexpectedly, Smith himself gets the job and happens to also have ten coins in his pocket. Smith’s belief that “The man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket” is true, justified, and believed, but it is true only due to an unforeseen coincidence. Thus, it does not qualify as genuine knowledge.

Knowing extends far beyond this propositional framework. The deep history and incredible diversity of human knowledge encompasses at least three distinct but interrelated modalities: propositional knowledge (*knowing that*), practical knowledge (*knowing how*), and experiential knowledge (*knowing by acquaintance*). Consider the act of restoring a degraded ecosystem: one might possess propositional knowledge about ecological principles and biodiversity, practical knowledge of how to propagate native plants or control invasive species, and experiential knowledge of how an ecosystem responds over time to restoration efforts. None of these forms of knowing can be fully reduced to the others, yet they combine to create genuine expertise. This multifaceted nature of knowing highlights the limitations of purely propositional accounts of knowledge and points toward a more subtle understanding of our cognitive capabilities. The integration of these different forms of knowing (theoretical, practical, and experiential) more accurately reflects the integrated and complicated ways we navigate and understand the world. This suggests that any complete epistemology must account for all three dimensions of knowledge acquisition and application. Relevance extends to teaching, learning, and the academic endeavour.

In the following sections, I explore the philosophy of knowledge. I begin with an evolutionary perspective, tracing how our capacity for knowledge emerged from basic sensory mechanisms honed by natural selection, resulting in the diversity of creatures[^1_3] we know today (@sec-epistemology-evolution-sensation). The shared evolutionary lineage underscores that the ability to sense, process, and respond to the environment is a universal characteristic of life, not limited to creatures with nervous systems. This biological foundation is not simply a metaphor; it demonstrates that our entire philosophical framework about knowledge is grounded in the adaptive architectures shaped by evolution. The implication is that the nature of knowledge is contingent on the thing doing the knowing.

[^1_3]: The term *creature* originates from the Latin word *creatura*, which derives from *creare*, meaning “to create” or “to bring forth”. It first entered Middle English in the 13th century via Old French (*creature*) and carries a strong theological undertone as something created by God. In its earliest usage, creature often referred to us, people, reflecting the Judeo-Christian worldview where we are seen as the pinnacle of God’s creation. Over time, the term broadened to include all living beings, and even inanimate entities, conceived as products of creation.

This evolutionary lens offers a segue into the rapidly advancing field of artificial intelligence (AI). Just as human neural systems were shaped by evolution to make sense of the world, AI systems are being designed to process and interpret data—though through fundamentally different mechanisms. The question remains: can AI ever replicate or exceed the kind of *knowing* rooted in the adaptive, embodied, and experiential context of human cognition? Do AI entities *understand*? While AI today lack the embodied sensory experience of living organisms, they do interface with the world through artificial sensory mechanisms such as cameras and sensors. Yet, as we will see later (@sec-epistemology-evolution-sensation), certain forms of knowing (such as that tied to the human lived experience) may require more than simply sensing the world; they may depend on the integration of sensory input with an adaptive, embodied presence. This inquiry bridges the ancient origins of knowledge with its potential future and insists that we rethink the limits of knowledge, what it means to truly *know*, and *who or what* is doing the knowing.

Building on an empirical foundation, people have developed increasingly abstract and more useful ways of knowing (@sec-epistemology-scepticism and @sec-epistemology). Religious and mystical traditions provided early frameworks for understanding the world, but their resistance to revision and lack of verifiability ultimately limited their utility for systematic inquiry. Rationalist approaches grounded in pure reason and logical deduction lead to mathematics and logic but struggled to reconcile theoretical constructs with physical reality. Meanwhile, empiricism, with its emphasis on knowledge derived from sensory experience, grappled with challenges in establishing the reliability of perception and justifying the principles of inductive reasoning.

The scientific method resulted from a practical synthesis of these approaches. It combines empirical observation with rational analysis and pragmatic validation, all the while recognising that all knowledge is provisional. But this synthesis raises its own philosophical questions: how do we justify our trust in scientific instruments that extend our senses far beyond their natural limits (@sec-epistemology-technology)? What distinguishes scientific confidence from religious faith (@sec-faith-and-trust-in-technology)? How do we balance the competing demands of theoretical elegance, experimental evidence, and the ever-changing socio-cultural norms?

Modern epistemological frameworks (from constructivism to critical theory) have further complicated our understanding of knowledge production by highlighting the social and political dimensions of knowing. These perspectives tell us that knowledge never exists in a vacuum but always emerges within specific historical and cultural contexts. They challenge us to consider how power dynamics, social norms, and personal biases shape what we know and how we know it. They also remind us that knowledge is not a static entity but a dynamic process of negotiation and contestation. At the same time we must contemplate what to do in an age when knowledge is increasingly generated by but by machines and not the human mind (@sec-contemporary-challenges-and-future-directions).

This chapter maps this uneven terrain while maintaining focus on a central question: how can we best align our ways of knowing with the fundamental goal of understanding reality? Through careful examination of various epistemological approaches, their strengths and limitations, we seek not absolute certainty but rather increasingly reliable and useful ways of comprehending our world.

The journey through these epistemological schools reveals that knowledge is neither purely objective nor wholly subjective, but rather emerges through the disciplined application of multiple complementary approaches to understanding. This recognition of epistemological pluralism, properly constrained by empirical validation and logical coherence, offers our best path forward in the continuing quest to know.

To assist our journey, I have created a table that links some of the most influential philosophers. The table presents my modest attempt to create an ambitious intellectual genealogy of epistemological thought. It traces the evolution of how humans have conceptualised knowledge acquisition from Classical Greece through to the contemporary era. I try to display the interconnections between different philosophical traditions and their historical contexts.

The table is designed to illuminate four important dimensions of epistemological development: the philosophers themselves, their core positions, the web of influences connecting their ideas across the ages, and the cultural-historical matrices from which their thoughts emerged. Taking such a multidimensional approach allows us to see how epistemological frameworks didn't simply succeed one another in linear progression, but rather engaged in complex dialogues across time and space.

What is striking is the gradual fragmentation of epistemological certainty. We begin with the confident rationalism of Plato and the empirically-inflected realism of Aristotle, trace the emergence of systematic skepticism through figures like Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus, and witness the increasingly sophisticated challenges to simple notions of truth and knowledge as we move toward contemporary thought. The inclusion of more recent actors like Lyotard, Foucault, and Haraway shows how modern epistemology has become inextricably entangled with questions of power, perspective, and social construction.

The table's attention to the cultural-historical context is especially important. This prevents us from falling into the trap of treating philosophical ideas as if they emerged in some rarefied intellectual vacuum. Instead, we see how epistemological positions developed in dialogue with their times -- whether that's Al-Ghazālī wrestling with the relationship between reason and faith in the Medieval Islamic Golden Age, or Kuhn developing his paradigm theory against the backdrop of Cold War big science.

The table serves as both a reference tool and an argument about the nature of epistemological development itself. Its structure suggests that understanding how we know things requires understanding the complex interplay between individual thinkers, intellectual traditions, and broader historical forces. It's highlights how epistemology isn't simply about abstract theories of knowledge; instead, this field of philosophy is about how humans, embedded in particular times and places, have attempted to make sense of our ability to make sense of the world.

```{=tex}
Al-Ghazālī (1058–1111) & Islamic philosophy; skepticism about philosophical causation and sense reliability & Dialogues with Aristotelianism (Avicenna), influenced by Islamic theology (Ash'arism), and prefigures Hume's critique of causation. & Medieval Islamic Golden Age, cross-cultural transmission of Greek philosophy into Islamic thought, tension between reason and faith. & \emph{The Incoherence of the Philosophers} (1095) \\[1em]

Meister Eckhart (1260–1328) & Christian Mysticism; intuitive/experiential knowledge grounded in theology & Connected to Neoplatonism, influenced later mystical traditions (John of the Cross, Sufi mysticism parallels) and some phenomenological thought. & Late Medieval Holy Roman Empire, thriving monastic and scholastic culture, emphasis on spiritual renewal and mysticism. & \emph{Sermons} (early 14th century) \\[1em]

Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) & Renaissance Skepticism focusing on human judgment limits & Influenced by Pyrrhonism and classical sources, prefigures modern skepticism (Hume), engages with Reformation-era debates over truth. & French Renaissance, religious conflicts (Reformation), printing press spreading new ideas, skepticism as intellectual honesty. & \emph{Essays} (1580) \\[1em]

Francis Bacon (1561–1626) & Early Modern Empiricism, Scientific Method & Sets stage for modern science, bridging Renaissance humanism and mechanical philosophy; influences Locke, Newton, Royal Society. & Late English Renaissance, Elizabethan/Jacobean England, emerging scientific societies, decline of Aristotelian scholasticism. & \emph{Novum Organum} (1620), \emph{The New Atlantis} (1627) \\[1em]

Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) & Empiricism, Materialism & Engages with Baconian empiricism and Descartes' rationalism, influenced Enlightenment political thought (Locke, Spinoza). & English Civil War era, tension between royalists and parliamentarians, rise of mechanical philosophy and secular politics. & \emph{Leviathan} (1651) \\[1em]

René Descartes (1596–1650) & Rationalism, Methodological Skepticism & Interacts with Scholasticism and sets foundation for Enlightenment rationalism; Kant's transcendental idealism responds to Descartes. & Early Scientific Revolution, Catholic Europe (France/Netherlands), seeking secure foundations after religious conflicts. & \emph{Discourse on the Method} (1637), \emph{Meditations on First Philosophy} (1641) \\[1em]

Antoine Arnauld (1612–1694) \& Pierre Nicole (1625–1695) & Cartesian Logic, Rational Analysis of Ideas & Part of the Port-Royal circle interacting with Descartes, Pascal, Jansenism; influenced logic and epistemology in Enlightenment. & Seventeenth-century France, height of Cartesian influence, religious debates (Jansenism) and the rise of rationalist logic. & \emph{Logic, or the Art of Thinking} (1662) \\[1em]

Robert Boyle (1627–1691) & Early Experimental Philosophy, Empiricism & Connects Baconian empiricism with mechanical philosophy; influences Newton and the Royal Society. & English Restoration, founding member of Royal Society, era of experimental natural philosophy. & \emph{The Sceptical Chymist} (1661) \\[1em]

John Locke (1632–1704) & Empiricism (Tabula Rasa) & Responds to Descartes, influences Berkeley, Hume, and Enlightenment liberal political theory. Isaac Newton (1642–1726/1727) & Empirical-Mechanical Philosophy, Mathematical Physics & Integrates empirical observation with mathematical frameworks, building on Bacon, Boyle; influences Enlightenment epistemology and Kant. & Late 17th-century England, Royal Society milieu, Scientific Revolution pinnacle, establishment of universal laws and rational mechanics. & \emph{Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica} (1687) \\[1em]

Pierre Bayle (1647–1706) & Philosophical Skepticism, Religious Tolerance & Advanced sceptical philosophy by challenging the rationalist and dogmatic claims of his era; influenced later Enlightenment thinkers like Voltaire and Hume with his critiques of certainty and advocacy for toleration. & Late 17th-century France and the Netherlands; context of religious conflict post-Revocation of the Edict of Nantes, flourishing of early Enlightenment intellectual thought. & \emph{Dictionnaire Historique et Critique} (1697) \\[1em]

Giambattista Vico (1668–1744) & Historicist Epistemology, early Constructivist elements & Engages with Enlightenment rationalism but emphasises cultural-historical relativity; foreshadows hermeneutics (Dilthey) and Constructivist thought. & Early Enlightenment Naples, debate over the universality of reason vs. historical contingency, reaction to Cartesian method. & \emph{The New Science} (1725) \\[1em]

George Berkeley (1685–1753) & Idealism (to be is to be perceived) & Responds to Locke's empiricism, influences Hume and later phenomenalism; engages with early Enlightenment debates on material substance. & Anglo-Irish context, tension between materialist science and religious ontology, post-Newtonian philosophical developments. & \emph{A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge} (1710) \\[1em]

David Hume (1711–1776) & Empiricism, Radical Skepticism about Induction & Influences Kant, skeptical about causation and induction, links to Scottish Enlightenment and emerging naturalism. & Scottish Enlightenment, commercial society, declining religious authority, rising secular intellectual culture. & \emph{A Treatise of Human Nature} (1739–1740), \emph{An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding} (1748) \\[1em]

Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) & Transcendental Idealism, Synthetic A Priori Knowledge & Mediates between rationalism and empiricism, inspiring German Idealists and shaping modern epistemology. & Prussian Enlightenment, Frederick the Great's court, peak of rational debate, responding to Hume's skepticism and Newtonian physics. & \emph{Critique of Pure Reason} (1781/1787) \\[1em]

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770–1831) & Dialectical Method, Historical Determinism & Developed the dialectical method, emphasising the synthesis of contradictions; influenced statistical thinking in terms of modelling dynamic processes and understanding historical trends as interconnected developments. & Early 19th-century Germany; German Idealism, Napoleonic era, emerging focus on systematic philosophy and historical analysis. & \emph{Phenomenology of Spirit} (1807), \emph{Science of Logic} (1812–1816), contributions to the philosophy of history and systems thinking. \\[1em]

William Whewell (1794–1866) & Inductive Epistemology, Philosophy of Science & Developed systematic principles for inductive reasoning; contributed to the debate between empiricism and rationalism, influencing Mill and early scientific methodology. & Victorian Britain; scientific revolution and the institutionalisation of science, early tensions between natural theology and secularism. & \emph{The Philosophy of the Inductive Sciences} (1840), \emph{History of the Inductive Sciences} (1837) \\[1em]

John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) & Empiricism, Utilitarian Epistemology, Logic of Induction & Builds on Hume and Bacon, influences logical positivism, pragmatism, and social science methodology. & Victorian Britain, industrial revolution, social reform debates, rise of utilitarian political philosophy. & \emph{A System of Logic} (1843) \\[1em]

Karl Marx (1818–1883) & Materialist Conception of History, Ideology Critique & Influences critical theory, historical materialism affects epistemology of social sciences; responds to Hegelian idealism and classical economics. & Industrial revolution Europe, class struggles, mid-19th-century socialist movements, collapse of feudal structures. & \emph{The German Ideology} (writ. 1845–46, pub. 1932), \emph{Das Kapital} (Vol.1 1867) \\[1em]

Helena Blavatsky (1831–1891) & Esoteric/Theosophical Epistemology, Controversial Claims & Intersects with Western occult traditions and Eastern religious influences; marginal to mainstream philosophy but indicative of esoteric syncretism. & Late Victorian Britain and Russian intellectual contexts, colonial encounters with Eastern religions, spiritualist movements. & \emph{The Secret Doctrine} (1888) \\[1em]

Wilhelm Dilthey (1833–1911) & Hermeneutics, Historical Epistemology & Influences phenomenology, hermeneutics (Gadamer), and historicist critiques of positivism; contrasts with Enlightenment universalism. & Wilhelmine Germany, rise of historical and cultural sciences, reaction to positivist historiography and Comtean sociology. & \emph{Introduction to the Human Sciences} (1883) \\[1em]

Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) & Pragmatism, Fallibilism & Foundation of Pragmatism, influences James, Dewey, and logical empiricists; bridges logic, semiotics, and scientific methodology. & Late 19th-century America, post-Civil War intellectual expansion, growth of scientific institutions and professional philosophy. & \emph{The Fixation of Belief} (1877), \emph{How to Make Our Ideas Clear} (1878) \\[1em]

William James (1842–1910) & Pragmatism, Practical Justification of Belief & Connects empiricism and religious experience; influences American philosophy, resonates with Dewey and later neopragmatists. & Gilded Age America, rise of psychology as a discipline, religious pluralism, intellectual ferment in universities. & \emph{The Varieties of Religious Experience} (1902), \emph{Pragmatism} (1907) \\[1em]

John Dewey (1859–1952) & Pragmatism, Instrumentalism in Education and Knowledge & Influences education reforms, connects evolutionary theory with epistemology, linked to progressive political thought. & Progressive Era America, institutionalisation of public education, industrial economy and social reform movements. & \emph{How We Think} (1910), \emph{Experience and Nature} (1925) \\[1em]

Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) & Phenomenology (rigorous science of consciousness) & Influences Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty, Derrida, connecting with hermeneutics and existentialism; reaction to positivism and psychologism. & Austro-Hungarian Empire/German context, late 19th–early 20th century, crisis of foundationalism in math/logic. & \emph{Logical Investigations} (1900–1901), \emph{Ideas} (1913) \\[1em]

Jean Piaget (1896–1980) & Constructivism (Genetic Epistemology) & Links developmental psychology and knowledge theory, influencing educational psychology, interacting with Kantian and empiricist currents. & Early to mid-20th century Swiss intellectual climate, rise of developmental psychology and scientific study of cognition. & \emph{The Child's Conception of the World} (1929), \emph{Genetic Epistemology} (1970) \\[1em]

Herbert Marcuse (1898–1979), Max Horkheimer (1895–1973), Theodor Adorno (1903–1969) & Critical Theory (Frankfurt School), reason as domination and social critique & Connects Marxism, psychoanalysis (Freud), and Weberian social critique, influencing Habermas, feminist and postcolonial theorists. & Interwar Germany, Weimar to Nazi era, exile in US, post-WWII Western reconstruction, responding to mass culture and capitalist modernity. & \emph{Dialectic of Enlightenment} (Horkheimer \& Adorno, 1944), Marcuse: \emph{One-Dimensional Man} (1964) \\

Karl Popper (1902–1994) & Critical Rationalism, Falsification & Engages with logical positivism and Vienna Circle, influences philosophy of science debates (Kuhn), stands against dogmatic certainty. & Interwar and post-WWII Europe/Britain, Cold War era science policy, British empirical tradition vs. Continental philosophy. & \emph{The Logic of Scientific Discovery} (1934), \emph{The Open Society and Its Enemies} (1945), \emph{Objective Knowledge} (1972) \\[1em]

Konrad Lorenz (1903–1989) & Evolutionary Epistemology & Connects biological evolution with knowledge acquisition, influences ethology, relates to Popper’s evolutionary approach to knowledge. & Early-mid 20th century Austria/Germany, rise of ethology, aftermath of Darwinian theory’s integration into behavioural sciences. & \emph{Behind the Mirror} (1973) \\[1em]
```

<!-- ## From Sensation to Understanding: Evolution of Knowing {#sec-epistemology-evolution} -->

## Pre-Cognitive Epistemes {#sec-epistemology-evolution}

[All sections here are incomplete and need to be expanded.]

### The Evolution of Sensation {#sec-epistemology-evolution-sensation}
Pre-cognitive sensing emerged approximately 3.5 billion years ago with the advent of life itself. During the early stages of life's beginning, 'knowing' had one sole purpose: adaptation rather than reason. Prokaryotes navigated their environments exclusively through molecular engagement with chemical gradients and, later, with light. For roughly 1.5 billion years, prokaryotes refined their chemo- and phototactic responses absent from any form of neural mediation and attained a level of precision rooted in evolutionary optimisation rather than cognitive computation. These cells were (and continue to be) 'concerned' about nutrients, toxins, and signaling molecules to guide their movements and maintain homeostasis. They also responded to basic physical variables like temperature or pH.

This era of early sensory evolution defies the notion that the advanced knowledge systems needed to infer success onto the individual require neurons; instead, it reveals that effective and useful environmental integration can occur through molecular machinery alone. We see information processing resulting in immediate reaction (to a stimulus), not conceptual understanding. In one sense, evolution through natural selection is pragmatism (@sec-epistemology-pragmatism) in action at the most fundamental level: if a molecular mechanism can solve a problem, it will be selected for; if not, it is eliminated as future options.

The capacity of early cyanobacteria to detect and respond to light gradients exemplifies this point. Their photoreceptive pigments were not precursors to neural systems, but fully realised molecular solutions that channeled energy into metabolic processes. These mechanisms altered Earth’s atmosphere through oxygenic photosynthesis (setting the stage for all subsequent stages of evolution), yet they never involved conceptual understanding. As eukaryotic life emerged around 2 billion years ago, cellular complexity and signaling pathways diversified, but even then the fundamental character of these responses remained pre-cognitive. Organisms integrated multiple environmental cues through intricate molecular interactions, producing complex behavioral outcomes devoid of neural input.

The implications are profound. In these ancient systems, responses arise through precise molecular architecture rather than neural networks or learned behaviour. Their optimisation depends on selection over deep evolutionary time rather than on conscious adaptation. Such sophistication at the molecular level, persisting to this day, demonstrates that pre-cognitive sensory mechanisms are not mere transitional forms. They represent a stable and enduring mode of environmental engagement that stands alongside the more recently evolved neural frameworks of later life. By examining these ancient mechanisms, it becomes clear that knowledge need not be confined to sentient or conceptual forms; pre-cognitive systems, operating at a molecular scale, prove capable of integrating environmental information with an efficacy that challenges our traditional hierarchies of cognitive evolution. In doing so, they compel us to broaden our definition of knowledge to include diverse, non-neural forms of environmental awareness that emerged long before the advent of consciousness.

### A Philosophical Perspective {#sec-epistemology-evolution-philosophical}

While ancient philosophers lacked knowledge of prokaryotic sensing mechanisms, **Aristotle**’s (384--322 BCE) concept of physis -- the intrinsic principle guiding the development and behavior of living entities -- offers a framework for understanding life’s inherent capacity to engage with its environment. In *Physics*, Aristotle asserts that natural things possess an original internal principle (*archē*) of motion toward some completion (*telos*), distinguishing them from artificial objects. He states, “Nature is a source or cause of being moved and of being at rest in that to which it belongs primarily” (Physics II.1, 192b20–23). In other words, he recognised that all living organisms have an innate drive toward their natural ends, aligning with the idea that even the simplest forms of life possess inherent mechanisms enabling environmental interaction. This thread of thinking lay largely dormant until the theory of evolution and advances in molecular biology provided mechanisms to explain such innate capacities. Pre-cognitive sensing systems, which emerged at the dawn of life, may precisely embody what Aristotle termed *physis*: the inherent principle of environmental engagement encoded not in abstract reasoning but in the molecular architecture of living systems themselves.

**Konrad Lorenz** (1903--1989) provided a bridge between Aristotle's *physis* and modern evolutionary understanding by grounding the idea of innate, goal-directed principles in the framework of natural selection. In *Behind the Mirror* (1973), he made the case that knowledge systems fundamentally emerge as adaptations to environmental constraints, shaped by the evolutionary pressures that favour survival and reproduction. Accordingly, even the most basic forms of sensory engagement (i..e even chemical sensing) represent evolutionary solutions to the challenges posed by the environment. These adaptations form an innate 'knowledge' of reality, not in the conceptual or reflective sense, but as a deeply embedded responsiveness that enables life to thrive. Even the earliest mechanisms for sensing and responding to the environment represent enduring, elegant solutions rather than simply stepping stones to more complex cognition.

In *The Open Society and Its Enemies* (1945) and *Objective Knowledge: An Evolutionary Approach* (1972), **Karl Popper**'s (1902--1994) proposed that knowledge evolves through a process of *conjecture* and *refutation*, the core of the scientific method. It does not require a big leap in imagination to extend this process to molecular processes goverened by evolution by natural selection. The molecular mechanisms of chemotaxis, for example, is a direct analogue of Popper's "survival-tested" concept. Each random mutation in sensing proteins represents a 'conjecture' and the reality of natural selection provides the 'refutation'. Molecular configurations not selevted by nature were eliminated and successful variants persisted and propagated.

Popper emphasised *incremental* evolution. Molecular sensing mechanisms didn't emerge fully formed but underwent countless iterations of molecular refinement. Each slight improvement in protein structure or signaling pathways withstood Popper's "selection pressures", except, here it operates at the molecular rather than conceptual level. Popper proposed that knowledge evolves through "natural selection on mental representations". Though bacteria possess no neurons in which to form mental representations, their molecular machinery serves an analogous function and encodes billions of years of evolutionary 'wisdom' in the exact architecture of proteins and signaling pathways.

Far from mere philosophical analogy, this parallel suggests that Popper inadvertently described a universal principle of knowledge evolution, one that operates from molecular mechanisms to scientific theories. The pre-cognitive sensing systems of early life thus serve as both historical precursor and proof of concept for Popper's evolutionary epistemology.

In **Donald T. Campbell**'s (1916--1996) essay *"Evolutionary Epistemology"* (1974 and onwards), he argued that human cognition evolved through a process of evolution by natural selection, much like biological traits. He suggested that our sensory and cognitive systems, including knowledge itself, are structured by evolutionary pressures geared toward adapting to an environment. He also introduced the notion of "blind variation and selective retention" in the context of epistemic processes, suggesting that our understanding of the world is shaped by this mechanism.

**Louis C. Helm** (????) and **William W. Dressler** (????) further explored how knowledge itself might evolve in accordance with evolutionary theories, contributing to the idea that cognition, including basic survival mechanisms like sensory input, represents rudimentary forms of knowledge in earlier organisms before our more complex treatments of belief and understanding emerged.

This synthesis of philosophical insight and modern evolutionary understanding reveals that the capacity for environmental engagement isn't something added to life but rather intrinsic to it from the very beginning. The pre-cognitive sensing mechanisms of early life thus represent not just the historical origin of knowing but a fundamental pattern that persists throughout the evolution of knowledge systems.

In this light, we might view the entire history of knowledge systems as elaborations on a theme first articulated by Aristotle's *physis* and fully realised in our understanding of pre-cognitive molecular mechanisms. These ancient systems reveal that knowledge, in its most fundamental form, emerges from the direct interaction between life and environment, shaped by evolutionary pressures rather than conscious design.

### Non-human Knowing: Beyond Posthumanism to Prehumanism

Defining knowledge as existing beyond human consciousness requires placing biological reality within philosophical frameworks. **Donna Haraway** (b. 1944) and **Timothy Morton** (b. 1968) take a position against our default anthropocentric epistemological stance and explore ideas that align with **post-humanist** thought. This approach decentres human consciousness and provides a foundation for understanding as something inherent in the interconnectedness of all life forms.

Haraway’s concept of **situated knowledge** provides the theoretical framework for understanding diverse forms of engagement with the environment. Haraway’s critique is primarily directed at human scientific practices, but it can be extended to consider how molecular mechanisms like those in *Deinococcus radiodurans* are adaptive forms of knowing. Its radiation resistance could be seen as a form of **embodied knowledge**, a kind of understanding encoded directly in molecular machinery without conscious awareness. Thus, she challenges the disembodied, objective knowledge that traditionally dominates Western epistemology and favours the materiality and context-dependence of knowledge production.

Though Haraway does not explicitly identify her work as posthumanist, her ideas align with this perspective. Her essay *A Cyborg Manifesto* (1985) critiques anthropocentrism and explores the relational entanglements between people, nonhuman animals, machines, and ecosystems. Her terms, such as ‘companion species’ and ‘sympoiesis’, show her preference for describing interconnectedness and the mutual processes through which life and knowledge systems are constituted.

Morton’s ecological thought, specifically the concept of the **mesh**, frames non-human knowledge systems as integral components of extensive, interconnected ecological networks. The mesh emphasises the relational nature of all entities, revealing bacteria like *Thermus* spp. not as isolated organisms but as participants in complex environmental interdependencies. Their thermal adaptations, far from survival mechanisms, point to their active role in maintaining and responding to ecosystems shaped by forces that transcend traditional human scales.

In Morton’s concept of **hyperobjects** (phenomena like geothermal heat, planetary cycles, or climate change that operate across spatial and temporal dimensions beyond immediate human perception), *Thermus* spp. participate in processes that exceed local survival. These bacteria, with their capacity to function at extreme temperatures, demonstrate how life integrates into and influences systems that exceed our ability to grasp at the vast spatiotemporal scales they operate at. In this view, bacterial adaptations are not isolated traits but active engagements within the broader ecological mesh.

Posthumanism critiques human-centric epistemology but often remains reactive to humanism, framing knowledge and existence regarding how humans come to understand them. I argue that a **prehumanism** perspective goes further. It eliminates residual human-centric tendencies by recognising forms of knowledge that precede and transcend human consciousness entirely. It acknowledges evolutionary and ecological modes of understanding that flourished long before human cognition emerged.

From this perspective, the **anthropic principle** -- that the universe’s observed conditions must allow for the existence of observers—serves not as a validation of the human perspective but as an instructive irony. It simply states that we exist in a universe compatible with our emergence, not that our existence or epistemological frameworks are central to the cosmos. Instead, the anthropic principle highlights the contingency of human perception as a latecomer to epistemic processes embedded in material and ecological systems billions of years before our species arose. This recognition requires that we not simply to decenter human consciousness but that we concede that sophisticated knowledge systems existed long before (and entirely independent of) the relatively recent accident of human beings capable of reflecting on knowledge.

Prehumanism also offers interesting implications for interpreting the anthropic principle. Rather than suggesting the universe is fine-tuned for conscious observers, we might better understand it as fine-tuned for knowledge production in all its forms, from quantum interactions to molecular sensing to neural processing. Human consciousness becomes not the pinnacle of cosmic awareness but one manifestation among many of the universe's inherent capacity for knowing.

The molecular machinery of prokaryotes exemplifies this pre-human epistemology. These systems do not merely challenge human exceptionalism; they demonstrate that complex knowledge production and environmental integration existed long before the evolution of neurons. Prokaryotic sensing and response mechanisms represent not primitive precursors to consciousness but refined endpoints of evolutionary optimisation.

Although pre-humanist, embodied knowledge systems (such as genetic codes, neural wiring, and symbiotic network responses) may appear maximally optimised, they remain provisional in a fundamental sense. Their functional correctness is contingent upon relatively stable environmental envelopes. When these envelopes widen or narrow -- due to climate change, new predators, shifting resource distributions, or other ecological pressures -- what was once an adaptive ‘knowledge solution’ can become obsolete. Just as human intellectual frameworks must be revised in light of new evidence or theoretical challenges, biological know-how accumulates only insofar as it maximises ecological fitness. Over evolutionary timescales, natural selection perpetually revises, refines, or discards these knowledge forms. What emerges is not an absolute, unchanging truth but a continuous adaptation process. In this light, even the most deeply embodied, nonhuman modes of knowing are provisional, dynamically sculpted by shifting ecological circumstances.

Can this reframing influence scientific investigation? Understanding non-human forms of knowing requires new methodological approaches that can account for distributed, ecological forms of knowledge production. It even extends to AI. New experimental paradigms could capture the complexity of non-human sensing and response systems and acknowledge their embeddedness in more extensive networks, networks that existed long before human observation.

### Understanding

In @sec-epistemology-evolution-sensation, I discussed the preconditions for human understanding. So far, I have used the term *understanding* almost interchangeably with *knowledge*, implicitly assuming we share a common definition. However, I have yet to explicitly define or argue for what understanding truly entails. Let us now dig deeper and develop a clearer understanding of understanding.

The relationship between knowing and understanding represents a multifaceted challenge. Knowing emerges as distinct modalities (propositional, practical, and experiential understanding; see @sec-knowing) but understanding comes out of a higher-order synthesis that transcends these individual components. This synthesis doesn't only aggregate different forms of knowledge; it transforms them into a coherent, integrated framework that enables deeper comprehension and more effective action.

Understanding manifests in the scientific practice. A marine biologist studying temperate reef ecosystems draws upon propositional knowledge of reef ecology, practical knowledge of sampling methodologies, and experiential knowledge gained through countless hours of field observation. But their understanding of reef systems goes far beyond these individual knowledge components. It emerges as a dynamic, integrated perspective that enables them to grasp complex interactions, predict system responses, and develop effective conservation strategies.

This integration process isn't just additive. Understanding arises through the knowledge modalities informing and enriching each other. Propositional knowledge provides theoretical frameworks that help interpret practical experiences. Practical knowledge grounds theoretical insights in concrete reality. Experiential knowledge reveals nuances and complexities that refine both theoretical models and practical approaches. The result is a sophisticated comprehension that exceeds the sum of its parts.

The contextual and relational nature of understanding becomes evident in addressing complex challenges. Climate change, for instance, demands more than accumulated knowledge about atmospheric physics, ecological impacts, and mitigation strategies. True understanding requires grasping the intricate web of relationships between physical processes, biological responses, and human systems. This integrated comprehension enables more effective responses to environmental challenges.

Understanding's transformative potential manifests powerfully in educational contexts. Traditional education often emphasises knowledge transmission, but genuine learning requires nurturing the integration of different knowledge modalities. When students engage with material through multiple approaches—theoretical study, practical application, and direct experience—they develop deeper understanding that enables creative problem-solving and innovative thinking.

From a philosophical perspective, understanding represents a distinct epistemological achievement. While knowledge can be compartmentalized and transmitted in discrete units, understanding emerges through active synthesis and integration. It requires not just knowing facts or procedures but grasping the underlying principles, relationships, and contexts that give them meaning. This distinction has profound implications for how we approach both research and education.

The evolution from knowledge to understanding often follows a non-linear path. Initial exposure might begin with propositional knowledge, but deep understanding typically emerges through iterative cycles of theoretical reflection, practical application, and experiential learning. This process reveals understanding's dynamic nature. It continually evolves as new insights and experiences reshape our comprehension.

Understanding's relational aspect extends beyond connecting different forms of knowledge. It encompasses relationships between concepts, between theory and practice, and between knowledge and its broader contexts. This web of relationships enables the recognition of patterns, the anticipation of consequences, and the generation of novel insights, capabilities that mere knowledge accumulation cannot provide.

## Foundation of Critical Thinking: Scepticism and Cartesianism {#sec-epistemology-scepticism}

At its core, scepticism is not so much a way of knowing as a philosophical stance toward knowledge claims. It functions as a methodological approach that can be applied within any epistemological framework. It is a call to question and validate knowledge rather than generate it. The development of many epistemological schools of thought themselves owes much to the influence of sceptical philosophers. From Pyrrhonian doubt to Cartesian methodological scepticism to modern scientific scepticism, it has evolved into a over-arching meta-epistemological mindset -- it serves as a second-order approach that evaluates and interrogates all ways of acquiring knowledge. It is this role that makes scepticism and Cartesianism indispensable to modern scientific inquiry.

The historical roots of formal scepticism trace back to **Pyrrho of Elis** (*c*. 360--270 BCE), the founder of Pyrrhonism. His encounters with Eastern philosophies during his travels to India inspired his systematic approach to doubt. Pyrrho proposed that since our senses and reasoning can deceive us, we should suspend judgment about truth claims, advocating for *epoché* ("suspension of judgment") as a methodological principle. This early form of scepticism laid the groundwork for later developments in philosophical and scientific thought.

While Pyrrho himself likely did not use the term *epoché*, **Sextus Empiricus**, writing in the late 2nd or early 3rd century CE, formalised and articulated this concept as central to Pyrrhonian scepticism in *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*. This is the essence of Pyrrho’s approach to achieving *ataraxia* (tranquillity). Sextus’s analysis of the limitations of sensory evidence and reasoning continues to inform contemporary approaches to measurement error and observational bias, particularly in the study of systems with complex interactions where causation is difficult to establish.

Medieval Islamic philosophy, through figures such as **Al-Ghazālī** (1058--1111), presented thoroughly logical arguments questioning causation. In his 1095 work Tahāfut *al-falāsifa* (*The Incoherence of the Philosophers*), Al-Ghazālī posed epistemological challenges to the notion of necessary causation, arguing that causation is not inherent in the nature of things but a matter of divine will. These ideas prefigured David Hume’s (@sec-epistemology-empiricism) later critique of causation in Western philosophy.

The Renaissance period brought significant transformation to sceptical thought through **Michel de Montaigne** (1533--1592). His collection of 107 essays across three books, titled *Essays* (first published in 1580), demonstrated how sceptical thinking could enhance rather than impede inquiry and established principles that would later influence hypothesis testing and scientific peer review. Montaigne’s embrace of systematic doubt provided a framework for critically examining assumptions while encouraging productive investigation.

The most systematic response to sceptical challenges emerged through Cartesianism, a term derived from the Latinised form of **René Descartes**’ (1596--1650) name, *Cartesius*. In his *Discourse on the Method* (1637) and *Meditations on First Philosophy* (1641), Descartes transformed scepticism from a potentially paralysing philosophical stance into a constructive methodology. Central to his work is the principle that the only thing beyond doubt is the existence of the thinking self: *cogito, ergo sum* (“I think, therefore I am”).

Descartes reasoned that the act of doubting requires a doubter, something that is thinking. Thus, the very act of thought demonstrates the existence of the thinker. “I think” refers to the undeniable act of thinking (whether doubting, reasoning, or imagining) and “therefore I am” affirms the existence of a thinking self, as thought cannot occur without a thinker. This fundamental principle, known as the *cogito*, provided a secure starting point for rebuilding knowledge on unshakeable foundations. Descartes’ methodological scepticism, which demanded that all knowledge claims be subjected to rigorous doubt, laid the groundwork for modern scientific inquiry.

Descartes was particularly concerned with the proper application of human reason. As he wrote in *Discourse on the Method*:

::: {.cell}
```{=tex}
\epigraph{
\begin{quotepara}
For it is not enough to possess a good mind; the most important thing is to apply it correctly. The greatest minds are capable of the greatest vices as well as the greatest virtues; those who go forward but very slowly can get further, if they always follow the right road, than those who are in too much of a hurry and stray off it.
\end{quotepara}
}
```

```{=html}
<div style="font-size: smaller;">
For it is not enough to possess a good mind; the most important thing is to apply it correctly. The greatest minds are capable of the greatest vices as well as the greatest virtues; those who go forward but very slowly can get further, if they always follow the right road, than those who are in too much of a hurry and stray off it.
</div>
```
:::

Starting from radical doubt, Descartes sought to rebuild knowledge systematically, emphasising clarity and precision. This fundamentally influenced scientific thinking. **Nicolas Malebranche** (1638--1715) expanded on these ideas in *The Search After Truth* (1674–1675) and highlighted how systematic doubt could serve as a positive tool for inquiry. Similarly, **Antoine Arnauld** (1612--1694) and **Pierre Nicole** (1625--1695), in *Logic, or the Art of Thinking* (1662), also known as the Port-Royal Logic, applied Cartesian principles to scientific reasoning and showed how clear and distinct ideas could enhance logical and empirical inquiry.

The influence of Cartesian methodology extends past its historical context. Descartes’ emphasis on breaking problems into manageable parts, working methodically from simple to complex, and demanding clear and distinct ideas continues to underpin scientific methodologies. Modern experimental design, with its focus on controlled variables and systematic investigation, owes much to this Cartesian legacy, which remains central to critical thinking and inquiry today.

The Scientific Revolution marked a sharp transition in sceptical thought, integrating it as a cornerstone of scientific thinking. The Royal Society, founded in 1660, underscored this commitment by adopting the motto *Nullius in verba* ("Take nobody’s word for it"), symbolising its dedication to empirical scepticism and the rejection of dogmatic authority. Natural philosophers like **Robert Boyle** (1627--1691) developed methodological approaches that successfully combined sceptical rigour with empirical investigation and so established the foundations for modern scientific practice.

The seeming friction between sceptical thought and scientific progress gave rise to two interesting philosophical responses: **fallibilism** and **relativism**. Fallibilism stems from the Latin word *fallibilis*, meaning "liable to err" or "capable of being mistaken". Developed by **Charles Sanders Peirce** (1839--1914), is the principle that no belief is beyond doubt or revision. Peirce concedes that while absolute certainty may be impossible, we can still develop reliable knowledge through rigorous methodology. This position offers a practical resolution to sceptical challenges by accepting the possibility of error while maintaining that scientific knowledge, though tentative, can be both reliable and useful. We see this approach reflected in modern statistical inference and confidence intervals, tools that explicitly acknowledge uncertainty while enabling meaningful scientific conclusions.

Relativism is a more radical. Thomas Kuhn (see @sec-epistemology-constructivism-postmodernism) makes the case that scientific truth claims are inherently relative to their paradigmatic context, thus attempting to sidestep sceptical challenges altogether. This stance risks undermining the objective aspirations of scientific inquiry and many philosophers of science tend to favour fallibilism's more nuanced position.

Contemporary scientific scepticism, cuttingly articulated by voices of reason such as **Carl Sagan** (1934--1996) in *The Demon-Haunted World* (1995), emphasises the essential role of disciplined doubt in scientific progress. His principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence provides a practical framework for evaluating research findings. This is especially important in complex biological systems where multiple variables interact. His words have never been more relevant than today:

::: {.cell}
```{=tex}
\epigraph{
\begin{quotepara}
I have a foreboding of an America in my children's or grandchildren's time -- when the United States is a service and information economy; when nearly all the manufacturing industries have slipped away to other countries; when awesome technological powers are in the hands of a very few, and no one representing the public interest can even grasp the issues; when the people have lost the ability to set their own agendas or knowledgeably question those in authority; when, clutching our crystals and nervously consulting our horoscopes, our critical faculties in decline, unable to distinguish between what feels good and what's true, we slide, almost without noticing, back into superstition and darkness...

The dumbing down of American is most evident in the slow decay of substantive content in the enormously influential media, the 30 second sound bites (now down to 10 seconds or less), lowest common denominator programming, credulous presentations on pseudoscience and superstition, but especially a kind of celebration of ignorance.
\end{quotepara}
}{Carl Sagan \\ The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark (1995)}
```

```{=html}
<div style="font-size: smaller;">
```
